stimulus.title: Evaporation from skin
stimulus.text: Researchers placed 1.0 g of each liquid on a patch of skin and measured how far the skin temperature fell as it evaporated.

table.caption: Drop in skin temperature as 1.0 g of liquid evaporated

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Describe the relationship between heat of vaporization and the drop in skin temperature shown in the table.

rubric.point: States that a higher heat of vaporization goes with a larger drop in skin temperature.
accept: the larger the heat of vaporization, the more the skin cools

parts.sample: Liquids with a higher heat of vaporization cooled the skin more: water, with the highest value, lowered skin temperature the most.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the heat, in joules, removed from the skin when 2.0 g of water evaporates.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why water has a higher heat of vaporization than acetone, even though both are polar.

rubric.point: Water molecules form hydrogen bonds with each other and acetone molecules do not, so each escaping water molecule must break more or stronger attractions.
accept: hydrogen bonds must be broken for water molecules to escape

parts.sample: Water molecules hold each other with hydrogen bonds, and a molecule must break all of them to escape as vapor. Acetone molecules cannot form hydrogen bonds with each other, so less energy frees them.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Predict how the drop in skin temperature would change if the water were applied on a humid day, when evaporation is slower, and justify your prediction.

rubric.point: Predicts a smaller drop (or a slower drop) because less water evaporates in the same time, so less heat is carried away.
accept: smaller temperature drop because less evaporation removes less heat

parts.sample: The skin would cool less in the same time. With slower evaporation, fewer water molecules leave per minute, so less heat is carried away from the skin.
